turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Dr. Smith. Nice to meet you too. Um, so, I'm here because, well, it's just getting to be way too much, honestly. I'm in school right now, taking some college classes and doing my clinicals to be a radiologic technologist. Which is great, I really like the field, but the problem is... well, whenever I’m supposed to just sit still, whether it's in a long lecture in the classroom or, especially, when I'm in the radiology suite observing or waiting for the next patient, I literally feel like I am crawling out of my skin. 

And I mean that physically. It's this intense, awful feeling. You know how those imaging rooms are, they're kind of dark and quiet, and everyone else is just sitting at the monitors perfectly fine, but my whole body is just screaming at me to do something. I’ve been trying to tough it out for months now. I kept telling myself, 'Just focus, just sit in the chair, you're 18, you're an adult, you can just stand there like a normal person,' but it doesn't work. No matter how hard I try to force myself to just be still, I still end up pacing around the control area, or shifting my weight constantly from one foot to the other, or bouncing my leg so hard I'm probably annoying everyone around me. 

I'm constantly finding some excuse to move, too. Like, I'll tell the techs I need to go check the lead aprons, or restock the sterile wipes, or I'll pretend I need to use the bathroom for the fourth time in a morning just so I can walk down the hallway and burn off some of that energy. I just can't stay put, and it's exhausting trying to hide it every single day.

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient describes constantly shifting their weight and bouncing their leg.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient reports leaving their seat to pace or finding excuses to walk down the hallway when they are expected to sit still.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly describes an intense physical feeling of restlessness, stating they feel like they are 'crawling out of my skin' when expected to be still.

turns.doctor_question: When you feel this need to move, do you feel an overwhelming sense of internal anxiety or dread that only goes away when you start moving?
turns.patient_response:
No, it's not really like anxiety or dread. I mean, I know what anxiety feels like—like before a big anatomy exam when you're sweating and your heart is racing and you're worried you're going to fail and ruin your whole career before it even starts. It's not like that at all. It’s more like... well, it’s like my muscles themselves just have this built-up pressure in them. Like a physical tension, you know? 

It's not that I'm scared something bad is going to happen if I don't move. It's just that if I sit there for too long, my body starts feeling like a coiled spring that's been pushed down way too tight. It's almost like an itch, but inside my bones, if that makes any sense. And the only way to scratch it, the only way to release that physical pressure, is to get up and walk around or shake my leg or just do *something*. So, yeah, it's not a mental dread or a panic attack or anything like that, it's just this intense, physical drive where my body is basically demanding to be put into motion.

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient describes needing to 'shake my leg' to release the built-up physical pressure.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient states that they have to 'get up and walk around' to relieve the physical tension of sitting too long.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly describes an internal feeling of restlessness, stating their body feels like a 'coiled spring' with an 'intense, physical drive' demanding motion.

turns.doctor_question: Does this intense urge to move your body change depending on the time of day, specifically becoming more noticeable or difficult to manage when you are trying to relax in the evening or right before you go to sleep?
turns.patient_response:
No, not really. I mean, it’s not like it suddenly gets worse right when the sun goes down or when I’m getting into bed. It’s pretty much just a constant thing whenever I’m forced to be inactive, no matter what the clock says. Like, if I have a morning lecture at 8 AM, I’m bouncing my leg and feeling that tension. If I have an afternoon clinical rotation at 2 PM, I’m pacing the control room. 

I guess when I get home in the evening, I’m usually so exhausted from trying to hold it all in all day that I just kind of collapse, you know? But even then, if I sit down on the couch to try and watch a movie or something, I can’t just *sit* there. I have to be doing something with my hands, or shifting around, or getting up to grab a snack even if I’m not hungry, just to have an excuse to move. But it’s not like it’s a specific "evening" problem. It’s not like those commercials for restless leg syndrome where people say it only happens when they lie down to sleep. For me, it’s just... if I’m awake, and I have to be still, my body hates it. Morning, noon, or night, it doesn't matter. It’s just the stillness itself that’s the problem, not the time of day.

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient describes bouncing their leg, doing something with their hands, and shifting around.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient mentions getting up to grab a snack just to have an excuse to move when they are supposed to be sitting.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes a constant tension and states that their body hates being still, indicating a persistent feeling of restlessness.
symptom_reasoning.S013: The patient notes an inability to just sit and watch a movie or relax on the couch without needing to move.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back at your time in elementary or middle school, did you struggle with this same need to move or difficulty sitting still in class, or is this something that only started more recently?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, man, no, this is definitely not a new thing. Not at all. It's funny you ask about elementary school, because, honestly, if you ask my parents about it, they’ll probably just groan and roll their eyes. They still talk about it. It’s like this running joke in our family, except it wasn't really funny at the time. 

I mean, I remember being in, like, second or third grade, and it was just constant. Every single parent-teacher conference, it was the exact same story. The teachers would sit my mom and dad down and say, "He’s a smart kid, but he just will not stay in his seat." And it was true! I’d be up sharpening my pencil five times during a spelling test, or I’d be walking over to the trash can to throw away a tiny scrap of paper, or I’d just be standing at my desk while everyone else was sitting, because sitting just felt impossible. 

And it wasn't just the moving around, either. The teachers were always getting on my case because I’d be blurting things out. Like, they’d ask a question, and before they even finished the sentence, I’d just shout out the answer without raising my hand. I just couldn't hold it in. Or we’d be doing a worksheet, and the teacher would be up at the front explaining how to do the first problem, and I’d already be halfway down the page, just rushing through it, not even listening to the directions because I just wanted to get it done and get moving. 

So, yeah, this whole thing with the radiology suite and the clinicals... it's really just the adult version of what I was doing back when I was seven years old. It’s the exact same feeling, just in a different setting. It’s been happening way, way before middle school, and definitely way before I ever thought about going into radiology. It’s just... it’s always been like this. I was always the kid who couldn't sit still, the one who was always rushing ahead, always calling out. It's just who I've always been, I guess.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient describes frequently leaving their seat in elementary school, such as standing at their desk or getting up to sharpen pencils when they were expected to remain seated.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly states they would shout out answers before the teacher had even finished asking the question.

turns.doctor_question: Beyond the physical restlessness and the tendency to blurt things out, do you also find that you frequently struggle to maintain focus on tasks, often lose things, or find it difficult to organize your daily responsibilities?
turns.patient_response:
No, honestly, not really. I mean, my focus is actually pretty good, especially when I'm at work or in the middle of a clinical rotation. Like, I don't zone out when I'm positioning a patient or setting up the equipment. I'm actually really locked in during those moments because there's so much going on and I have to be precise, you know? 

And as far as losing things... no, I'm actually kind of meticulous about my stuff. I have to be. In this field, you can't just be misplacing your dosimeter badge or losing the lead markers you need for the X-rays. I always know exactly where my keys are, where my phone is, where my ID badge is. I have this whole system when I get home where everything goes into a specific bowl by the door, and I never deviate from it. If I didn't do that, maybe I'd lose things, but because I have that routine, it's never really been an issue.

And organizing my responsibilities... I mean, I manage a full class schedule, clinicals, and studying. I use a planner, I color-code my shifts versus my lectures, and I always get my assignments in on time. I don't forget appointments or double-book myself. It's just... the actual sitting down to *do* the studying is where the physical part gets me. Like, I know exactly what chapter I need to read, and I know when the test is, and I have all my highlighters lined up, but my body is just screaming to get out of the chair while I'm trying to read the textbook. 

So, yeah, it's really not a mental organization problem or a forgetfulness thing. I don't walk into a room and forget why I went in there, and I don't lose my train of thought in the middle of a conversation—unless I'm getting really distracted by how much I need to stretch my legs. It's really just the physical motor constantly running, the blurting things out, the rushing... but the actual focus and keeping track of my life? That part I actually have a pretty tight grip on.
